title: Rooftop Gardens
summary: How gardens on roofs cool buildings and cities, grow food, shelter wildlife, and soak up rain, and what builders must plan to make them work.
poll: Every school should have a garden on its roof.

versions.title: Gardens on Top
versions.text:
Look up at that roof. Do you see green? It is a garden! It is on top of a house.

A city can get very hot. Roads soak up the sun. So do walls. Then they give off heat.

Plants on a roof help. They make shade. The soil blocks the heat, too. So the rooms below stay cool. That saves power.

Plants drink water. Some goes out of the leaves. It goes into the air. That cools the air.

You can grow food up there. Grow a vegetable like a tomato. Grow mint for tea.

Bees and birds come to the plants. They find food. They find a home.

Rain falls. The soil soaks it up. So less water floods the streets.

But a roof garden needs care. Wet soil is heavy. So the roof must be strong. It must not leak. Pick plants that need just a bit of water.

In Saudi Arabia, lots of roofs are flat. That is a good spot for a garden. Riyadh plans to plant lots of trees, too.

In Saudi Arabia, many roofs are flat. They are a good place for gardens. Riyadh also plans to plant millions of trees.

versions.title: Rooftop Gardens
versions.text:
Look up at the top of a tall building, and you might see green leaves and bright flowers. Around the world, people are turning empty roofs into gardens.

Cities can get very hot. Concrete buildings and dark roads soak up sunlight all day long. Then they slowly give off that heat, so a city can stay warm even at night.

A rooftop garden can help. The plants shade the roof, and the soil acts like a blanket that blocks heat from the sun. As a result, the rooms below stay cooler. People need less air conditioning, which saves electricity.

Plants also cool the air in another way. They pull up water through their roots, and some of that water leaves through tiny holes in their leaves. There, it evaporates, which means it turns into a gas. This takes heat from the air around the plants.

Families can grow food on a rooftop garden. They can grow a vegetable such as a tomato or a pepper, and they can grow fresh mint for tea.

Roof gardens also become a habitat, or home, for bees, butterflies, and birds.

When rain falls, the soil soaks it up, so less water rushes into the streets and causes floods.

But a rooftop garden needs careful planning. Wet soil is heavy, so the roof must be strong. Builders add a layer that stops leaks and another layer that lets extra water drain away. In a dry place, it is best to choose plants that need little water.

In Saudi Arabia, many houses have flat roofs, which are a good place for gardens. Riyadh also plans to plant millions of trees to help cool the city.

Look up at the top of a tall building, and you might see green leaves and colorful flowers instead of bare concrete. Around the world, people are transforming empty roofs into productive gardens.

versions.title: Rooftop Gardens: Cooling Cities from Above
versions.text:
Look up at the top of a tall building, and you might see green leaves and colorful flowers instead of bare concrete. Around the world, architects and families are transforming empty roofs into productive gardens that benefit both people and nature.

Cities are often several degrees hotter than the surrounding countryside, a pattern scientists call the urban heat island effect. Concrete buildings and dark roads absorb sunlight throughout the day and gradually release that heat, so a city can remain uncomfortably warm even at night.

A rooftop garden can reduce this problem. The plants shade the roof, and the soil provides insulation, acting like a thick blanket that slows the movement of heat into the building. Consequently, the rooms below stay cooler, and residents need less air conditioning, which saves electricity.

Plants also cool the air through a second process. They draw up water through their roots, and some of that water escapes through tiny openings in their leaves, where it evaporates and changes into a gas. Because evaporation requires energy, it removes heat from the surrounding air.

Families can grow food on a rooftop garden, cultivating vegetables such as tomatoes and peppers along with fresh mint for tea. These gardens also increase biodiversity, providing a habitat for bees, butterflies, and birds that find few green spaces in crowded cities. In addition, when rain falls, the soil absorbs much of it, so less water rushes into the streets and causes flooding.

However, a rooftop garden requires careful engineering. Wet soil is surprisingly heavy, so the roof must be strong enough to support it. Builders install a waterproof layer that prevents leaks and a drainage layer that allows extra water to drain away. In a dry climate, gardeners should select plants that need little water and use drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots.

Rooftop gardens are not a new idea, since people in several ancient civilizations planted gardens on terraces and roofs. Today, cities such as Toronto require green roofs on certain large new buildings, while Singapore offers support to owners who add them.

In Saudi Arabia, many houses have flat roofs, which are an excellent location for gardens, and the Green Riyadh project plans to plant millions of trees to help cool the capital.
